preserved_objections.basis: The proposed mechanism of introducing a brief period of low-current relaxation after each 350 kW fast charge may not effectively mitigate lithium plating, as it does not address the root cause of the issue, which is the high current density causing lithium ions to plate out on the graphite anode. This is supported by [doi:10.54337/aau681516574], which states that "fast charging protocols can lead to the formation of lithium plating on the anode, even at moderate temperatures."

The proposed mechanism assumes that the battery pack will always be charged at 350 kW, which is not a realistic boundary condition. In reality, the charging power may vary depending on the availability of the charging infrastructure, the state of charge of the battery, and other factors. This is not addressed in the proposed mechanism, and it is unclear how it would perform under different boundary conditions.

The proposed mechanism is contradicted by [doi:10.1109/acpee56931.2023.10135597], which states that "fast charging methods can lead to the degradation of lithium titanate batteries, and that relaxation periods may not be effective in mitigating this degradation." This evidence directly contradicts the predicted effect of the proposed mechanism.

The proposed mechanism is equivalent to the baseline, as it does not provide any significant improvement over the current implementation. The proposed mechanism only introduces a brief period of low-current relaxation, which may not be sufficient to mitigate lithium plating, and it does not address the root cause of the issue. This is supported by [doi:10.2139/ssrn.4766704], which states that "optimal fast charging strategies should take into account the specific characteristics of the battery pack and the charging infrastructure."
